title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
question: Why does the Moon change shape?
answer: The Moon never really changes shape. It is always a round ball, and the Sun always lights up half of it. As the Moon travels around Earth about once a month, we see different amounts of that bright half. That is why it looks thin, then half, then full, and then thin again.

visual.what: Night on a balcony. Bối points at a thin crescent Moon, and Beo pretends to munch a giant cookie. Huy laughs while Hùng holds up a photo of last week's full Moon.

parts.text: Huy, look! Two weeks ago the Moon was a big round ball. Now it is a thin banana! Did someone take a bite?
Maybe a giant ate it for breakfast!
Nobody is eating the Moon. And here is a surprise. The Moon is always a round ball. It never really changes shape at all!

visual.what: Huy faces the camera, with three small pictures floating beside him. They show the Sun, the Moon going around in a loop, and a row of Moon shapes.

parts.text: So why does it look so different from night to night? Today we will find out what lights up the Moon, where it travels, and why we see a new shape each night.

visual.what: Bối's guess drawn in crayon. The Earth casts a dark shadow that covers part of the Moon, with a big question mark next to it.

parts.text: I know! The Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon. That makes the dark bit.
That is a great guess, Bối. Lots of grown-ups think so too. And you are right that the Earth has a shadow.

visual.what: Beo's guess as a cosy cartoon. A sleepy Moon with a face pulls a starry blanket up over half of itself.

parts.text: I think the Moon goes to bed. It pulls up a blanket!
A sleepy Moon with a blanket! I love it, Beo. Guessing is how scientists start.

visual.what: Sun, Earth and Moon in a straight line, with the full Moon sliding into Earth's long dark shadow. It is labelled lunar eclipse, only at full Moon.

parts.text: Sometimes the Moon really does slide into Earth's shadow. That is called a lunar eclipse. But it can only happen at full Moon, and not every month. So the shadow is not why the Moon changes shape night after night.
So what is it then?

visual.what: On the left, a glowing Sun with rays coming out, labelled makes its own light. On the right, a grey Moon, labelled rock and dust, no light of its own. Hùng holds up a plain grey rock.

parts.text: Clue number one. The Sun makes its own light. The Moon does not. The Moon is a big ball of rock and dust, with no light of its own.
I brought a Moon rock! Well, a rock from the garden. It does not glow either.

visual.what: A dark room. Hùng shines a torch on a football, and only the side facing the torch is bright. Arrows show light going to the ball and bouncing to Bối's eyes.

parts.text: Then why does it shine so brightly at night?
Because sunlight lands on it and bounces back to our eyes. It is like a football in a dark room. You only see it when a torch shines on it.
Torch off, no ball. Torch on, there it is!

visual.what: The Sun on the left shines on a big Moon ball. The half facing the Sun is bright and labelled day, and the far half is dark and labelled night. A small Earth beside it is half lit too.

parts.text: The Moon is round like a ball. So the Sun can only light the half that faces it. That half is bright, like daytime. The other half is dark, like night.
Just like Earth! Half has day and half has night.

visual.what: A close-up of the Moon ball, half bright and half dark. A curved line between them is labelled terminator, the edge where day meets night. Beo stands beside it doing a stiff robot pose.

parts.text: Right! The line between the bright half and the dark half has a funny name. It is called the terminator.
Terminator? Is it a robot?
No robots, Beo. It just means the edge where day meets night.

visual.what: Huy faces the camera next to a big card that shows the Sun lighting one half of the Moon.

parts.text: So here is step one. The Sun always lights up one half of the Moon.

visual.what: The Earth in the middle, with the Moon travelling around it on a big dotted loop. Curved arrows show the way it goes, and the loop is labelled orbit.

parts.text: Clue number two. The Moon does not stay still. It travels around the Earth in a big loop. This trip is called an orbit.

visual.what: A calendar page with about 29 and a half days crossed off, and a little Moon shape drawn in each box. A big label says about one month.

parts.text: It takes the Moon about 29 and a half days to go through all its shapes and come back to the same one. That is about one month.
A whole month for the shapes to repeat?
Yes, Bối. The Moon's loop around Earth is enormous, and it takes about a month to go round.

visual.what: Beo stands in the middle of the room. Hùng walks in a circle around him, always facing him, and wobbles at the end with little dizzy stars over his head.

parts.text: Here is something odd. The Moon always shows us the same face. Hùng, walk around Beo and keep looking at him.
I only see your face! Never your back!
Round and round. Whoa, now the whole room is going round!

visual.what: The Moon at four spots around Earth, with the same smiley face always pointing at Earth. The hidden side is labelled far side.

parts.text: Exactly. Scientists call this tidal locking. It means the same side of the Moon always faces Earth. The other side is called the far side. We can hardly ever see it from here. The Moon wobbles a tiny bit, but most of the far side stays hidden.

visual.what: Huy faces the camera, holding a card of the Moon going around Earth with the same face always pointing in.

parts.text: Step two. The Moon travels around Earth about once a month, always showing us the same face.

visual.what: A big picture seen from above. The Sun is on the left, Earth is in the middle, and the Moon is at several spots around Earth. Each Moon has its bright half facing the Sun, and a tiny child on Earth looks out.

parts.text: Now let us put the clues together. Wherever the Moon goes, the Sun lights the half that faces the Sun. But we are looking from Earth, in the middle.

visual.what: Sun, Moon and Earth in a line, with the Moon in the middle and its bright half facing the Sun. A box shows what we see from Earth, an almost black Moon labelled new Moon.

parts.text: When the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, its bright half faces away from us. We see only the dark half. That is the new Moon, and we can hardly see the Moon at all.
The Moon is still there, just hiding in the dark!
Peekaboo, Moon!

visual.what: The Moon a quarter of the way around Earth, at the side. A box shows what we see from Earth, half a circle lit, labelled half Moon.

parts.text: About a week later, the Moon has gone a quarter of the way around. Now we see half of its bright half. It looks like half a circle. We call it a half Moon.

visual.what: The Moon on the far side of Earth from the Sun, with its bright half facing Earth. A box shows a big round bright Moon, labelled full Moon.

parts.text: About a week after that, the Moon is on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun. Now the whole bright half faces us. Full Moon!
The big round one!

visual.what: Bối looks worried and holds two drawings, a small Moon and a big Moon. Huy holds up a whole ball, half painted yellow.

parts.text: Wait. So the Moon is not really getting smaller?
Not one bit. The Moon is always a whole ball, and half of it is always lit. What changes is how much of that bright half we can see from Earth.

visual.what: Huy faces the camera, pointing at an eye on Earth looking at a half-lit Moon.

parts.text: Step three. The shape we see depends on where the Moon is in its trip, and how much of its sunny half points at us.

visual.what: Hùng holds up a long chart of eight Moon shapes, numbered 1 to 8, from new Moon to waning crescent. At first he holds it upside down, then flips it the right way.

parts.text: Scientists give the shapes names. There are eight main phases. A phase just means the shape the Moon seems to have on that night.
Here is the chart! Oops, it is upside down. There we go.

visual.what: Side by side, a thin crescent Moon next to a banana, and a gibbous Moon next to a round full tummy. Bối giggles and Beo grins.

parts.text: A crescent is a thin curved sliver, like Bối's banana. Gibbous is the word for a Moon that is more than half lit, bulging out like a full tummy.
Gibbous! That sounds like a name for a monkey!
Can I have a pet gibbous?

visual.what: The row of Moon shapes. An arrow going up from new to full is labelled waxing, growing. An arrow going down from full back to new is labelled waning, shrinking.

parts.text: From new Moon to full Moon, the bright part grows each night. We say the Moon is waxing. From full Moon back to new Moon, it shrinks. We say the Moon is waning.

visual.what: A giant clock face in the night sky with the eight Moon phases in place of the numbers. People from long ago point up at it.

parts.text: Then the whole pattern starts again, about every 29 and a half days. It is so regular that people all through history have used the Moon to count time, like a giant clock in the sky.

visual.what: Huy faces the camera next to a circle of the eight phases, with an arrow going round.

parts.text: Step four. The Moon goes through eight phases, growing and then shrinking, and the pattern repeats about once a month.

visual.what: A room with the curtains closed. Hùng puts a torch on a table and a grown-up stands nearby. Labels show torch is the Sun and ball is the Moon.

parts.text: Want to see the phases yourself? Ask a grown-up to help. You need a torch, a ball and a dark room. Put the torch on a table so it shines toward you. The torch is the Sun.
Torch ready, ball ready, curtains closed!

visual.what: Hùng stands in the room holding the ball out in front of him, a little above his head. A label on his head says Earth. The ball slips, and Beo catches it.

parts.text: Your head is the Earth. Hold the ball out in front of you, a little above your head. That ball is the Moon. And never stare straight into the torch.
Whoops, the Moon slipped!
I caught the Moon!

visual.what: Hùng turns slowly in a circle holding the ball up. Small pictures around him show the lit part of the ball as a crescent, then half, then full.

parts.text: I am turning slowly and the bright part of the ball is changing! Now a thin crescent. Now half. Now it is all bright!
You just made the phases of the Moon. The ball never changed. Only where it was changed.

visual.what: Bối and Beo at a window at night with a grown-up, drawing Moon shapes in a notebook with a grid of 30 boxes.

parts.text: Here is another try. With a grown-up, look at the Moon each night for a month and draw its shape. You will see it wax and wane, just like our chart.
I will draw a Moon every night!

visual.what: A simple summary picture. The Sun lights half of the Moon, the Moon goes around Earth, and a row of shapes shows what we see.

parts.text: So why does the Moon change shape? The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of that bright half.

visual.what: A new Moon seen from above. The side facing Earth is dark, but the far side facing the Sun is bright and sunny, with a little label that says not dark!

parts.text: And here is a fun fact. Some people call the far side the dark side of the Moon. But it is not dark! The Sun shines on it too. At new Moon, when we see no light at all, the far side is all lit up.
So the hidden side has its own sunny days!
Sunny on the back!

visual.what: A split picture with a blue sky over Earth on one side and a black sky over the Moon on the other. All four wave beside a big Subscribe to Ask Huy button.

parts.text: Next time, we will find out why the sky is blue here on Earth but black on the Moon. Subscribe to Ask Huy so you do not miss it!
Bye! Keep looking up!
Bye bye, Moon!

facts.claim: The Moon is a rocky and dusty place and does not make its own light; we see it because sunlight lights it.
Because the Moon is round, the Sun lights up half of it at a time.
The line between the lit and dark halves of the Moon is called the terminator, the edge between day and night.
A lunar eclipse can only happen at full Moon.
The cycle of phases repeats about every 29.5 days, about a month.
Because of tidal locking, the same side of the Moon always faces Earth. The other side is called the far side.
The Moon wobbles a little (libration), so we can sometimes see a small part of the far side.
At new Moon, the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, and we look at its unlit half.
First quarter, the half Moon, comes about a week after new Moon.
At full Moon, the Moon is on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun, and we see the whole lit portion.
There are 8 main phases. A crescent is a thin sliver, and gibbous means more than half lit.
Waxing means the lit part is growing, from new Moon to full Moon. Waning means it is shrinking, from full Moon to new Moon.
People throughout history have used the Moon's cycles to measure time.
The far side is sometimes called the dark side, even though the Sun does shine on it.
The sky on the Moon looks black even in the daytime because there is no atmosphere.

description: Why does the Moon look like a thin banana one week and a big round ball the next? Join Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo as they find out how sunlight, the Moon's month-long trip around Earth and our view from home make the eight phases of the Moon. It ends with a simple torch-and-ball activity that children can try with a grown-up.

cast.name: Huy
cast.role: the host (25): curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
